1:
The date is fixed by an event in the northern kingdom, and Gill reads it closely: the third year of Hoshea means the third year of his rebelling against Assyria, when he shook off the yoke and refused to be tributary any longer. Keil and Delitzsch set the reign in its whole arc. When the ten tribes were destroyed, Judah stood in a dependence on the imperial power of Assyria into which the ungodly policy of Ahaz had brought it; but three years before the expedition of Salmanasar against Samaria, Hezekiah had come to the throne of his ancestor David and set on foot with zeal the healing of Judah's wounds, exterminating idolatry and restoring the legal worship. Because he was devoted to the Lord with an undivided heart, they say, the Lord acknowledged his undertakings, so that when Sennacherib had overrun Judah and summoned the capital to surrender, the prayer of that faithful servant was heard and the proud army destroyed, leaving Assyria too weak for Judah to fear it much longer.

Henry is struck less by the reign than its unlikelihood. Hezekiah's father was one of the worst of the kings and he one of the best, which may intimate that whatever good there is in any man is not of nature but of grace, free grace, sovereign grace, which contrary to nature grafts into the good olive what was wild by nature (Romans 11:24). The disadvantages were real: Ahaz probably gave his son a bad education as well as a bad example, Urijah the priest perhaps had the tuition of him, and his companions may be supposed addicted to idolatry; yet he became eminently good, and Henry's conclusion is a question, that when God's grace will work, what can hinder it. He adds an observation about the timing, that the two ages put Hezekiah's birth when his father was eleven or twelve, so ordered that he should be of full age and fit for business by the time the measure of his father's iniquity was full.

That comparison is itself a difficulty, and Gill works at the arithmetic. Ahaz began to reign at twenty and reigned sixteen years, so died at thirty-six, which would make his son born to him at eleven. Grotius eases it by a year, since Hezekiah had only entered his twenty-fifth year and might be just turned twenty-four, putting his father at twelve; and Gill observes that the historian regularly drops or adds the incomplete years of kings, so Ahaz might have been near twenty-one at his accession and reigned almost seventeen, which makes him about thirty-eight and leaves nearly fourteen years between them. Even without that, he says, Bochart and others have collected instances enough of children begotten by men under that age. Wesley solves it differently, denying that Ahaz need have lived only thirty-six years, since the sixteen years of his reign may be reckoned not from his first accession, while he reigned with his father, but from the beginning of his reigning alone.

Two names in the notice draw comment. Ellicott finds the king's own name significant in this form, meaning that my strength is Jah, and thinks its special appropriateness exemplified by the history that follows (Psalm 18:2); of his mother's name he suspects a slip, since Abi should probably be Abijah, as in Chronicles and a few manuscripts. Keil and Delitzsch pass straight from the mother to the verdict, that as ruler he walked in the footsteps of his ancestor David, removed the high places and the other objects of idolatrous worship, trusted in Jehovah and adhered firmly to him without wavering, so that the Lord made all his undertakings prosper. Clarke, who summarises the chapter from the reforms to the insulting message at its close, declines to argue the chronology here and refers it back to his note on an earlier reign.
3:
The qualifying clause is what Gill and Henry both notice: other kings are said to have done right, but not like David, or as he did without doing all that he did, which is what is claimed here. Henry makes the point by contrast: David had many degenerate sons, some of whom did right without loving God's ordinances or cleaving to them as he did, whereas Hezekiah was a second David with the same love for God's word and house. He draws an encouragement against assuming that virtue must decay: it does not follow that when times and men are bad they grow worse and worse, since after many bad kings God raised up one like David himself. Clarke fills in the reformation: the priests and Levites cleansed the house his father had shut up and left polluted, a work of sixteen days, and since the passover could not then be kept in the first month Hezekiah published it for the second and gathered the men that feared God out of all Judah and Israel.

On the objects destroyed they sort into two classes. Gill observes that removing the high places is what the best kings of Judah had never attempted, a thing noted to their discredit, and Ellicott reads the emphatic construction the same way, that he it was who removed them, making the Temple the only place of public worship. He also sharpens the other terms, the images being rather shattered pillars and the groves the Asherah, probably plural with all the versions. Henry divides them by origin. The images and groves were downright idolatrous and heathenish, and were broken although his own father had set them up and been fond of them, since we must never dishonour God in honour to our earthly parents. The high places were different: prophets had used them and good kings connived at them, yet they affronted the temple, breached the law, and being out of the priests' inspection let idolatrous usages in. Wesley adds that the most of them went, or those the people most frequented, not every one.

The serpent is the hardest case, having the best warrant. Henry puts the paradox plainly: it was of divine institution and was broken for that very reason, having been abused. Israel had carried it into Canaan and kept it as a memorial of God's goodness in the wilderness; but when men began to worship the creature more than the Creator, those who would not take images from the heathen were drawn into burning incense to this one because God had ordered it and it had done them good. So Hezekiah showed them it was Nehushtan, nothing but a piece of brass, and, as Henry takes it from bishop Patrick, ground it to powder so that no fragment remained; whatever honour the serpent lost is abundantly made up where our Saviour makes it a type of himself (John 3:14). Good things, when idolized, are better parted with than kept. Wesley is careful about the incense: offered not as to a god but as to an instrument of mercy through which adoration was directed to God.

Ellicott defends the relic's antiquity: attempts to evade the plain force of the statement he calls futile, since the compiler clearly believed the serpent Mosaic. In Egypt the serpent symbolised the healing power of Deity, a symbolism repeated in the myth of Æsculapius, so that Moses taught by means suited to the people that healing lay with Jehovah and not with any god of Egypt. On the name both hesitate. Ellicott prefers the impersonal rendering, that it was called so, and thinks the name may denote great serpent rather than brass-god. Clarke notes that no version translated the word, that Jarchi takes it for contempt meaning no more than a brazen serpent, and that the Targum makes it the people's name, not the king's.
5:
The trust is defined by what it refused as much as by its object. Gill has him depending on the Lord as protector and defender with no reliance on idols as an arm of flesh, and notes that the Targum makes the object the Word of the Lord God, so that the trust was not in Nehushtan but in him whom the brasen serpent was a type of. Ellicott draws the same contrast, setting Hezekiah against the idolatrous kings who had trusted in the Nehushtan itself. Wesley makes the refusal political: he trusted without calling in foreign succours to establish or help him, which his father Ahaz had done and Asa before him. Henry puts the same point as a situation rather than a policy, since Hezekiah came to the crown with his kingdom compassed about by enemies and did not send abroad for help as his father had, but trusted the God of Israel to be the keeper of Israel.

The claim that none was like him raises an obvious difficulty, because the same is said of Josiah, and three of them answer it the same way. Keil and Delitzsch refer this verdict to Hezekiah's confidence in God, in which he had no equal, while Josiah is praised in the same words for conscientious adherence to the Mosaic law, so that they find no contradiction to argue about. Ellicott says it in a line, that one was pre-eminent in trust and the other in strict obedience, and he also corrects the second clause to read not of those before him but among them. Wesley adds the comparison himself: each excelled the other in several respects, and Hezekiah's advantage was that he fell on the work at the beginning of his reign, which Josiah did not, and undertook what none of his predecessors durst do in removing the high places, where Josiah only followed his example. Wesley further limits the comparison to the kings of Judah, since David and Solomon were kings of all Israel.

The clinging is distinguished from the trusting. Gill takes it of his worship and service, or as the Targum has it of the fear of the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch gloss it as adhering faithfully to Jehovah and never giving himself up to idolatry. Ellicott separates the two clauses as feeling and practice, holding fast being the one and keeping the commandments the other, with the commandments specially in view being those against polytheism. Henry makes perseverance the thing for which Hezekiah was a nonesuch, since some of his predecessors began well and fell off, while he clave to the Lord with a fixed resolution and, like Caleb, followed him fully, not merely abolishing idolatrous usages but making conscience of his duty in everything. Henry adds the courage it took, since abolishing idolatry risked disobliging his subjects into rebellion, and observes that a firm belief of God's all-sufficiency to protect and reward is what makes a man sincere and bold and vigorous in duty. Clarke simply numbers the character and its result: four things done, trusting, cleaving, not departing, keeping; and two things following, the Lord with him and prosperity wherever he went.
7:
Prosperity and presence are tied together. Gill notes that the Targum reads the help as the Word of the Lord being for him, and Henry turns the sequence into a rule: he was with God, and then God was with him, and having that presence he prospered in his wars, his buildings and above all his reformation, which went forward more easily than he could have expected. Those who do God's work with an eye to his glory and confidence in his strength may expect to prosper in it. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read the promise more narrowly. Ellicott renders it that wherever he would go forth he would prosper, and notes that going forth means any external undertaking and especially going out to war; Keil and Delitzsch say the Lord gave him success in all his undertakings and in the revolt itself.

What the revolt was gets a careful defence. Keil and Delitzsch supply the history: Ahaz had brought Judah into dependence on Assyria, and Hezekiah released himself by refusing further tribute, probably after Salmanasar had left Palestine and possibly not until after his death, which is why Sennacherib afterwards made war to subjugate Judah again. Ellicott warns against taking the notice chronologically, since the opening verses are a preliminary sketch of the whole reign, resumed at large later. Wesley reads it as the recovery of a right: Hezekiah shook off a yoke his father had wickedly submitted to and reassumed the full and independent sovereignty God had settled in the house of David.

Wesley then distinguishes the case from one that is blamed. Zedekiah is condemned for rebelling against Babylon on three grounds that do not apply here: he had bound himself by a solemn oath and covenant, which we do not read that Ahaz did; he broke a covenant he had made himself; and God had actually given the dominion of his land and people to the king of Babylon and commanded submission. Where Hezekiah is said to rebel, Wesley argues, the word means only a defection from a subjection formerly performed, which may sometimes be justly done, so the word does not of itself prove a sin. That it was none seems certain to him because God owned and assisted him in it and never reproved him for it, either in the message sent by Isaiah or afterwards, though he was particularly reproved for vain-glory and ostentation. Henry reaches the same conclusion by a shorter road: it is called rebelling because the king of Assyria called it so, but it was an assertion of rights that lay outside Ahaz's power to alienate, and when a man has thrown out the idolatry of the nations he may well throw off the yoke of their oppression, since the surest way to liberty is to serve God.

The Philistine campaign is read as a recovery rather than a conquest. Gill has them invading Judah in his father's time and taking many cities, which Hezekiah now recovered, driving them back to their own territories; Henry says the same and draws the parallel, that having purged out the corruptions his father brought in he might expect to recover the possessions his father lost, and notes that Isaiah prophesied of these victories. Keil and Delitzsch add the chastisement and its extent, the cities taken under Ahaz wrested back and the country laid waste as far as Gaza, the most southerly of the chief Philistine cities; and both they and Ellicott think the campaign followed Sennacherib's retreat. On the phrase about the watchtower and the fenced city there is agreement that it is comprehensive: Keil and Delitzsch read it as all the towns from the least to the greatest, Clarke as a proverbial expression meaning that he reduced every kind of fortification and nothing could stand before him, and Ellicott that the entire land of Philistia was ravaged by the Judean forces.
9:
The fall of Samaria has already been told once, and the first question is why it is told again here. Keil and Delitzsch answer it from the sources: the earlier account came from the annals of the kingdom of Israel, this one from the annals of the kingdom of Judah, where the catastrophe is introduced as an event memorable for the whole covenant-nation rather than for the north alone. Clarke says only that the history has been given before. Henry gives three reasons why it belongs in Hezekiah's reign, and the first is that it explains the zeal of the reformation, since the people saw what idolatry had brought on Israel; when a neighbour's house is on fire and one's own in danger, it is time to cast away the accursed thing.

His other two reasons are about Hezekiah himself. The ruin was something he much lamented but had no strength to prevent, for though the ten tribes had revolted from the house of David and vexed it as lately as his father's reign, they were of the seed of Israel and he could not be glad at their calamities. And it was what laid his own kingdom open, since the fall of the north made the invasion of the south a far easier undertaking. Henry prefaces all this with an observation about the rise of the power itself, which had now grown considerable though we never read of it until the last reign: such changes there are in the affairs of nations and families, the despicable becoming formidable while those that made a great noise and figure are brought low.

The dates and the grammar are worked over in detail. Gill reads the three years inclusively, taking the end of them to mean their beginning, as the phrase is used elsewhere, which is how the sixth year of Hezekiah can be the ninth of Hoshea. Ellicott defends the plural verb, that the Assyrians took the city, against the older versions which make it he took it, on the ground that Sargon and not Shalmaneser took Samaria; and he thinks Schrader too positive in calling the plural a certainly false pronunciation, since the verse appealed to as decisive says only that the king of Assyria took the city and does not name him. On the closing verse he corrects two small things, that the conjunction before all that Moses commanded should be dropped with all the versions, the phrase standing in apposition to the covenant, and that the last clause reads literally and hearkened not, and did not.

That last clause is where the reason for the ruin is lodged, and both Henry and Ellicott dwell on it. Henry notices the order of the two verbs: they would neither hear God's commandments nor do them, and many will be content to give God the hearing who will give him no more, whereas these, being resolved not to do their duty, did not care to hear of it either. Ellicott reports Thenius taking the remark for the theme of the whole historical abstract the compiler worked from, the sentence that suggested the long reflection in the previous chapter, and allows that such reflections may have been prompted by passages of the Law and the Prophets. Keil and Delitzsch, for their part, let the bare list of places stand, Halah and Habor by the river of Gozan and the cities of the Medes, without comment on any of them.
13:
The date is the chapter's hardest problem, and Ellicott refuses to smooth it. The fall of Samaria is fixed at 722 by the Bible and the Assyrian inscriptions alike, and that was Hezekiah's sixth year, so his fourteenth should be 714 or 713; but Sennacherib's monuments put the expedition against Judah and Egypt at 701. The divergence is remarkable and must not be explained away: the Assyrian documents are strictly contemporary and, where unbroken, in exactly the state in which they left the scribes' hands, whereas these books were compiled long after the events and have reached us through innumerable transcriptions. He adds the king's own style from his annals, a name meaning that the moon-god multiplied brothers, and that he was Sargon's son and invaded Judah in his third campaign. Gill dates it only relatively, eight years after the captivity of Israel. Wesley reads the sweeping claim about the cities as a universal particle used loosely, and takes the success as given by God for three purposes: to lift the invader up to a more shameful fall, to chastise a people guilty of manifold sins, and to make room for the deliverance God designed.

What Hezekiah did first is not what he is remembered for. Keil and Delitzsch record real preparations: the city fortified more strongly, and the fountain of the upper Gihon and the brook beside it stopped up to cut the besiegers off from water. Ellicott explains why the invader went to Lachish: it stood in the south-west corner of Judah near the Philistine border and commanded the high road to Egypt, and Egypt was his real object, so that mastering the fortresses of a Judah allied with Egypt secured his rear. Henry measures the loss in territory, the fenced cities and garrisons taken first and the rest falling in of course, with the confusion described by the prophet.

Then came the embassy, and nobody defends it. Gill traces the change of mind: Hezekiah had made provision to defend himself and encouraged his people not to be afraid, but seeing the fortified cities gone he was disheartened and judged it better to buy peace than expose his capital, betraying much weakness and distrust of the power and providence of God. Henry asks outright where Hezekiah's courage was and where his confidence in God, and why he did not advise with Isaiah before sending so crouching a message. Ellicott contributes a detail that makes the wording less abject than it reads: the word rendered offended is literally sinned and is the term the Assyrian inscriptions use constantly for revolts, and the phrase about what is laid on him is the monuments' own formula for tribute.

The sums do not agree either. Sennacherib's account says eight hundred talents of silver where this says three hundred, which Ellicott reconciles by the talent used, the light Babylonian standing to the heavy Palestinian as eight to three; the demand was also about a seventh less than Pul had exacted from Menahem. Wesley simply converts: above two hundred thousand pounds. Raising it emptied both treasuries, which Gill observes had been the resource of the kings of Judah in distress more than once before. Then the doors: Ellicott glosses the verb as trimming or stripping, the word used of Ahaz doing the like, and notes that Hezekiah took the gold he had himself put on the framework as well as the plating of the leaves. Henry alone offers a defence. The necessity being urgent, Hezekiah might make as bold with dedicated gold as David, whom he took for his pattern, had made with the showbread, and giving a part to preserve the whole was neither impious nor imprudent; his father had plundered the temple in contempt of it, whereas he, having repaid with interest what Ahaz took, only begged leave to borrow it again and meant to restore it in full.
17:
The money bought nothing, and the breach of faith is what they fasten on first. Gill notes the plain fact that the tribute was taken and the army sent anyway, three generals going against Jerusalem while the king kept up the siege of Lachish. Ellicott thinks the violation careless rather than calculated, as Josephus states it. Wesley reads a consequence into it, that by breaking faith the invader justified Hezekiah's revolt after the event and prepared the way for his own destruction. Henry refuses the title the man is given in the narrative: is this the great king, the king of Assyria? Never call him so, he says, but a base and perfidious man, worthy to be made infamous to all ages, who took money on a promise to withdraw and then marched on the capital without so much as returning it. Those are wicked men whose principle it is to make a promise binding no further than their interest goes; and Hezekiah had reason to repent a treaty that left him much the poorer and never the safer.

The three names are not names. Clarke, following Calmet, takes all three for offices: the first for him who presides over the tribute, a kind of chancellor of the exchequer; the second for the chief of the eunuchs; the third for the master of the wine cellar. Ellicott agrees that they are titles but corrects the sense of two. The first is rather the commander-in-chief, the Hebrew merely imitating an Assyrian word of Sumerian origin; the third, though it does mean chief cup-bearer as Hebrew, is only a Hebraised form of an Assyrian title for a chief officer, used of superior military commanders and staff officers. The second he cannot identify on the monuments, though the Hebrew suggests a chief eunuch or courtier who would travel with the commander as his scribe. Both note that the parallel names only the third, who was the spokesman.

Clarke supplies a campaign history that explains the detachment. The Assyrian troops seem to have been worsted before Lachish and obliged to raise that siege, moving on to sit down before Libnah; and while the king was there word came that Tirhakah of Ethiopia had invaded Assyrian territory, so that having to hasten home he sent a force to Jerusalem instead, carrying a fearful and bloody manifesto which required tribute, the surrender of the kingdom, and the captivity of king and people. The document came with the vilest insults and the highest blasphemies, Clarke says, and God interposed so that the evils threatened fell on the sender. Manifestoes of this kind, he observes, have seldom been honourable to those who issue them, and he adds a modern instance.

Where they stopped is itself a tactical fact. Clarke identifies the conduit as the aqueduct bringing water from the upper reservoir near the valley of Kidron, which they had probably seized to distress the city, and the fuller's field as where the washermen stretched their clothes to dry. Ellicott sorts out the pools, since the upper pool here, called Gihon elsewhere and lying on the Joppa road to the west, is not the upper pool inside the city that goes by the names of the artificial pool and the old pool, below which a further pool was dug in Hezekiah's own time. Then they called for the king in person, and Clarke suspects why: they wished him to come out so that they might get possession of him. Keil and Delitzsch say Hezekiah thought it beneath his dignity to treat with generals and sent out three ministers instead, the captain of the castle who had lately replaced Shebna, Shebna himself as secretary of state, and the chancellor. Henry calls the refusal prudence and adds the instruction they carried, not to answer that fool according to his folly, since they could not convince him but would certainly provoke him.
19:
The speech opens on a title, and the title is itself an argument. Keil and Delitzsch note that the Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian kings all assumed it, since the kings of conquered lands were their vassals, and Ellicott supplies a specimen from the monuments, where a king calls himself the great king, the mighty king, the king of multitudes, the king of the country of Asshur; Hosea, he adds, applies the title king of princes to the Assyrian. Henry reads the usage as idolatry, the speaker making an idol of the prince whose creature he was: God is the great King, but Sennacherib was in his eye a little god, and he meant to pass the same veneration to his hearers and frighten them into submission. To those who by faith see the King of kings in his glory, Henry answers, even the king of Assyria looks mean and little; and Wesley asks what the greatest of men are when they come to compare with God, or when God comes to contend with them.

Who delivered the speech is debated from the Assyrian side. Ellicott records that an earlier king sent an officer of this rank as envoy to Tyre, and reports two guesses at why this one spoke: Thenius supposes he knew Hebrew better than his companions, while Schrader argues it would have been beneath the commander's dignity and that such language would sound strange in a eunuch's mouth. On the opening question itself Clarke insists the insult is sharper than the translation shows. He takes the noun for a diminutive expressing the utmost contempt for Hezekiah's God, and renders it: what little, foolish, unavailing cause of confidence is this to which thou trustest? Keil and Delitzsch read the same force without the diminutive, as an exclamation of how vain and worthless the confidence is.

The next charge is insincerity. Keil and Delitzsch gloss it tightly: if Hezekiah speaks of counsel and might for battle, that is only a lip-word, coming from the lips and not from the heart, the seat of the understanding, and so a foolish and inconsiderate saying; and they prefer this text's verb to the parallel's as the more original. Ellicott puts it as an aside, thou hast said, a mere lip-word it was, meaning language the speaker knew to be false, like our own lip-service, and he adds that the margin here is wrong. Henry answers the charge on the facts, since Hezekiah really did have counsel and strength for the war, and all that Rabshakeh can do is turn it off with a slight, that the words are vain and the match unequal.

On Egypt all four agree that the taunt is true even though the taunter is not to be trusted. Keil and Delitzsch describe the broken reed as one that runs into the hand of anyone leaning on it and pierces it through, and note that the figure is well chosen because the Nile is rich in reeds; Isaiah, they add, had already pressed the same warning on the party that looked to Egypt for help. Clarke supplies the political fact behind the image, that Egypt had already been greatly bruised and broken by the Assyrian wars. Ellicott prefers cracked or flawed to bruised, since what is meant is a reed splitting and piercing the hand that rests on it, and notes that the expectations from Egypt are denounced elsewhere as implying want of faith in Jehovah. Henry extends the figure as the prophet does, so that the reed not only fails the man leaning on it but rends his shoulder, and then turns it on the speaker's master: Assyria had been exactly that to Ahaz, who trusted it and was distressed rather than strengthened. Those who trust any arm of flesh will find it no better than a broken reed, but God is the rock of ages.
22:
The cleverest stroke in the speech turns the reformation into evidence against the reformer. Keil and Delitzsch credit the skill while naming its source, since Rabshakeh avails himself of Hezekiah's reform from a heathen point of view and represents the abolition of the altars on the high places as an infringement of the reverence owed to God. Clarke calls it artfully malicious and separates out the three things insinuated at once: that in removing places where many of the people had in fact sacrificed to Jehovah, Hezekiah had offended Jehovah himself, had deprived his people of their religious rights, and could therefore expect neither the blessing of God nor the cooperation of his subjects. Ellicott adds the intelligence that makes the stroke possible, since the Assyrians evidently knew of the reformation; a vassal's proceedings were watched with jealous interest.

What is wrong with the argument is that it assumes the wrong kind of God. Henry puts it as a measurement: Rabshakeh measures the God of Israel by the gods of the heathen, who delighted in a multitude of altars and temples, and so concludes that confining a people to one altar must have given great offence. One of the best deeds Hezekiah ever did is thus misconstrued as impious and profane by a man who did not, or would not, know the law of the God of Israel; and Henry's comment is that we must not think it strange when what is really good and pleasing to God is represented by ignorant and malicious men as a provocation to him. Wesley says the same more bluntly, that the speaker talks boldly of things he does not understand, judging the great God by their petty gods and God's worship by the fancies of heathen who measured piety by the number of altars.

Whom the sentence addresses is uncertain in the text itself. Ellicott notes that it seems to turn abruptly from Hezekiah to his ministers and the garrison at large, but that the versions and the parallel passage have the singular, which he thinks probably original, Hezekiah being mentioned immediately afterwards in the third person to avoid ambiguity. Keil and Delitzsch report the opposite preference, since Thenius and Knobel and others keep the plural here, on the ground that what follows addresses Hezekiah directly. Ellicott also presses the literal order of the last clause, that before this altar shall ye worship, at Jerusalem, which states the principle at issue: the great altar of burnt offering was to be the one altar and Jerusalem the one city where Jehovah might be worshipped.

The taunt about the horses is read as a wager. Ellicott canvasses the renderings of the opening verb, which is rather to make a compact than to give pledges, literally to mingle with or have dealings with, while Gesenius explains it as joining battle and Cheyne prefers laying a wager; and he reads the whole as a sneer at Hezekiah's want of cavalry, an arm in which the Assyrians were pre-eminently strong. Keil and Delitzsch make the insult precise. The meaning is not that Hezekiah could not raise two thousand soldiers altogether, but that he could not produce so many men able to fight as horsemen; and the officer he is then challenged to repulse is described by a word meaning an under-vicegerent, the administrator of a province beneath a satrap, so that the smallest of the invader's subordinates is meant. Clarke paraphrases it as an insult outright, that if two thousand Assyrian horses were handed over Hezekiah could not find riders for them. Henry hears banter rather than argument, with the speaker falsely insinuating that Hezekiah has no men at all, or none fit to be soldiers, and ready to lay any wager that one captain of the least of his master's servants could baffle him and all his forces.
24:
The taunt about the officer is sharper in Hebrew than in the rendering. Ellicott reads the opening as a bare "and how", the thought being that since Hezekiah cannot do the one he certainly cannot do the other; turning away the face means repulsing a man or rejecting his demand; and what is offered is not one captain of the least of the servants but a governor who is himself one of the smallest, by which Ellicott thinks the speaker means himself. He adds that the title used to be derived from Persian but is now known to be Semitic, answering to Assyrian words for prefect and prefecture. The last clause he repunctuates, so that the sentence stops at servants and what follows is not a question but the ground of the folly: but thou hast put thy trust on Egypt for chariots and horsemen.

Then comes the claim that changes the speech's character. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the move: having as he imagined removed every ground of confidence, Rabshakeh adds that the Assyrian king too has not come without Jehovah, but was summoned by him to destroy Judah. Clarke explains what it was for: seeing that the Jews placed the utmost confidence in God, he wished to persuade them that Hezekiah's conduct had driven Jehovah from them and made him an ally of Assyria, so that no help could come from that quarter. Wesley gives the shortest verdict, that he neither owned God's word nor regarded his providence but forged the oracle to strike terror into king and people. Keil and Delitzsch add a textual note, that the parallel reads against this land where this has against this place, which they put down to an attempt to make the two clauses match.

Where such a claim could have come from is canvassed carefully. Ellicott lists the options: Michaelis supposed the king had consulted captive priests of the northern kingdom; others think a report of the Hebrew prophets' menaces had reached Assyrian ears; Thenius makes the words a mere inference from the expedition's success, which Ellicott rejects as too definite a form of words for that; and he allows there may have been a renegade prophet of Jehovah in the camp. Keil and Delitzsch incline to the second, that a report of prophets who had represented the invasion as a judgment from the Lord was turned to the speaker's own purposes. Henry says much the same but denies the speaker any sincerity in it: he did not himself think he had a commission, and by whom should he have had one, but made the pretence to amuse and terrify the people on the wall, and if he had any colour for it he took it from what he had heard of God's hand in the destruction of the ten tribes, reckoning his warrant for Jerusalem as good as his warrant for Samaria.

What makes the boast less eccentric is that invaders talked this way. Ellicott produces a parallel from the annals of the last king of Babylon, where a Persian conqueror claims the special favour of the chief god of the city, who foretells his march on it and goes with him, and claims to have offered daily prayers to two other gods to intercede with that one for him. From this it appears to have been customary for invaders to try to win the gods of the countries they attacked over to their own schemes. Ellicott calls the form of the oracle thoroughly authentic and sets beside it the words of Chemosh to Mesha on the Moabite Stone, telling him to go and seize a city against Israel. He ends with the irony, that a later prophecy shows how true the boast was in a sense far above the speaker's heathenish apprehension; and Henry draws the rule that many who have fought against God have pretended commissions from him.
26:
The request to change languages is a request for privacy, and all of them see why. Keil and Delitzsch say the boasting might well have impressed the people, so the ministers asked for Aramaean, which they understood, instead of Jewish, on account of those on the wall. Ellicott puts the fear precisely: many of the people had always worshipped at the high places and might well wonder whether there was not something in the allegation that Jehovah was incensed at their removal. Henry calls the request reasonable and agreeable to the custom of treaties, by which plenipotentiaries settle matters before anything is made public, but thinks the man had been misjudged, since the request only exasperated him and made him ruder than before. Clarke states the purpose flatly: this blasphemous caitiff meant to stir the people to sedition, so that city and king might be delivered into his hand.

The two languages are worth identifying. Keil and Delitzsch describe Aramaean as the speech of Syria and Babylonia and probably of the province of Assyria, possibly the speaker's own mother tongue even if the Assyrian court language was another dialect; its close affinity to Hebrew would have made Hebrew easy for him, just as Aramaean was intelligible to Hezekiah's ministers, while the people of Jerusalem understood only the Hebrew of Judah. Ellicott adds that Aramaic was then the language of diplomacy and commerce across western Asia, as the bilingual contract-tablets found at Nineveh prove. On the other name he is careful: calling the language Jewish occurs in only one other place, and the word Jew only in the later books, though Assyrian usage of the time supports the view that the people were already so called.

The refusal is where the embassy stops being diplomacy. Keil and Delitzsch report the scornful ground, that his commission was not to Hezekiah and his ambassadors only but to the people upon the wall, and Ellicott sharpens the wording into a question, whether it is to the king and his ministers that he was sent to speak these words. The men on the wall are the soldiers on guard. Henry calls what follows a breach of every rule of decency and honour, since instead of treating with the commissioners he menaces the soldiery, works on them to desert or mutiny, and threatens the last extremities of famine if they hold out. That threat is put in terms the sources handle gingerly. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the Masoretes replaced both coarse words with euphemisms. Clarke explains their point, that the besieged be apprised what holding Hezekiah's side will cost, while Ellicott says resistance will bring them to such straits that they will be glad of the vilest garbage, and Wesley that the speech was to tell them what miseries he would force on them.

Then the posture changes with the audience. Keil and Delitzsch are precise about the verb, which means not that he stood up or stepped forward but that he stationed himself, taking an attitude calculated for effect before crying aloud in Jewish, telling the people to hear the king of Assyria and not be led astray by Hezekiah into defending the city, since neither Hezekiah nor Jehovah could save them; and in the phrase about being delivered out of his hand, they note, the speaker has stopped speaking in his master's name. Ellicott takes the verb as coming forward, nearer the wall, and records that the versions and the parallel read words where this has the word. Clarke says the performance was intended to make the people revolt from their allegiance. Henry reports the tradition that the speaker was an apostate Jew, which would account for his readiness in it, and infers that if so his ignorance of the God of Israel was the less excusable and his enmity the less strange, apostates being commonly the most bitter of enemies.
29:
The speaker changes character here, and Ellicott notices it. Handed an opening by the ministers' unwary request, he was quick-witted enough to take instant advantage of it and come forward as a friend of the people; and Ellicott corrects the text to match, since all the versions but one read that Hezekiah cannot deliver them out of my hand, not his. The denial is then double: Hezekiah cannot save them himself, and Jehovah will not. Ellicott defends the second half against the charge that it sounds too Jewish for a heathen's mouth: a man who could speak Hebrew would almost certainly know the name of the god of the Jews, and would naturally assume that a king and his prophets would urge trust in the God whose sanctuary stood on Zion and who was bound to defend his own dwelling-place. Henry reduces the whole to its alternative, that the people must either bend or break.

The offer that follows is couched in a phrase nobody can quite place. Ellicott reports it literally as making a blessing with the invader, which the Targum and Syriac render making peace, and observes that the phrase occurs nowhere else; perhaps it rests on peace being generally concluded with mutual expressions of goodwill, and Gesenius holds peace a conception akin to blessing. Keil and Delitzsch take the word the same way, as weal and blessing concentrated, and read the clause about coming out as a demand for surrender from behind the walls, the invitation to eat one's own vine following as its consequence. Wesley paraphrases the terms as they would have sounded: on these conditions I will give you no disturbance, but suffer each of you to enjoy his own possession.

What the promise amounted to depends on the force of "until I come". Ellicott gives two constructions. On one, the country people who had taken refuge in Jerusalem are invited back to their farms until the Egyptian campaign is over, after which they will be moved, though a new home as good as the old will be given them. On the other, following a well-known idiom, the sense is that immediate surrender will bring no harm and they shall enjoy their own land until he removes them to a better. Thenius denies any reference to Egypt and has the invader posing as a father preparing to receive his dear children, which Ellicott plainly thinks absurd. Clarke reads the promise as calculated sedition: resistance makes destruction inevitable, and the conqueror will deal with them as with every nation he takes, but surrender buys transport to a land as good as their own. Ellicott adds two glosses, that the olive meant is the cultivated kind and not the oleaster that yields less and worse oil, and that the verb for Hezekiah's persuading may be read as pricking them on.

Henry takes the offer apart. He wonders with what face a man could propose an agreement bought with a present when his master had just broken the one Hezekiah bought with a great present, and asks whether the grossly perfidious can expect to be trusted; but he answers himself, that gilding the chain is enough to make the vulgar let you bind them. He examines the two advantages in turn. Imprisonment is an advantage because they shall eat every man of his own vine, though the property will be vested in the conquerors and the free use of it last just as long as the conqueror pleases, which is not explained now though it would be plain afterwards. Captivity is a greater advantage still, since they will be taken to a land like their own; and Henry asks what the better they would be for that, with nothing in it to call their own. He wonders that anyone should expect to prevail by suggestions so gross, except that the devil imposes on sinners this way every day.
33:
The closing argument contradicts the one made a few verses earlier, and Ellicott will not pretend otherwise. If the claim that Jehovah himself sent the invasion is to stand with this appeal to the helplessness of foreign gods, one would have to suppose that the god of each conquered nation had likewise favoured the Assyrian cause; but since what follows plainly implies the impotence of those gods against Assyria, Ellicott admits a verbal inconsistency and excuses it by the occasion, since a speaker would hardly be particular in an extemporised address whose sole aim was to work on the fears of his hearers. He then reconstructs the logic as it may have run: Jehovah, far from opposing us, manifestly favours our arms, and even if you believe otherwise, no matter, since he is not likely to prove mightier than the gods of all the nations that have fallen before us.

The cities named have histories, and Ellicott supplies them. Hamath and Arpad had been reduced by Sennacherib's father, and Sargon's own record says that the king of the Hamathites drew Arpad, Simyra, Damascus and Samaria into a revolt which was crushed in battle, the ringleader being taken and flayed alive in 720. Arpad he locates ten miles north of Aleppo. Sepharvaim had revolted with Babylon at the beginning of the same reign, though no account of its fall survives. He also considers what the question about the whereabouts of these gods implies, and thinks it may mean they were annihilated along with their temples and statues; the Assyrians did sometimes carry off the idols of conquered nations, but that need not have been invariable, and a prophetic passage suggests they were sometimes destroyed outright, as was likely enough when a city was stormed and burnt.

Two of the names defeat him. Hena and Ivah are absent from the parallel passage and wholly unknown, and as the text now stands the words look like two Hebrew verbs, which is how the Targum takes them, turning the clause into a question about who had made these peoples wander and carried them away. Hoffmann proposes that the two words are really one and should be read as an epithet of the city just named, the utterly perverted, a nickname given by the Assyrians for its folly in revolting a second time after being once subdued. Ellicott prefers the proper name, since Ava and the Avites are mentioned elsewhere and the versions support it. He also reports a dispute about the last clause, which Ewald would render not as a question about Samaria but as an exclamation, how much less have its gods delivered it out of my hand, while several versions keep the question; and Ellicott suggests that a different particle may have stood in the original text.

Whose hand is meant turns out to matter. Ellicott notices that the speaker talks as though he and his father were one man, which he thinks lends some support to Schrader's view that the successive Assyrian invasions were not kept quite distinct in the Hebrew tradition, though elsewhere he resists that suggestion on the ground that the narrative speaks generally of the king of Assyria and refers to fathers in the plural. Keil and Delitzsch state the conclusion the argument is driving at without comment: since not one of the gods named could rescue his own land from Assyria, Jehovah will be no more able to defend Jerusalem. Clarke answers it. The reasoning is that Sennacherib is greater than any god of the nations, and that Jehovah shall therefore be reckoned one of them; and Clarke calls the impudent blasphemy of the speech without parallel. What he admires is how it was met, since the affront was not properly against Hezekiah but against the Lord, and Hezekiah referred the matter to Jehovah himself, who punished the blasphemy in the most signal manner.
36:
The silence was ordered, and Keil and Delitzsch find two purposes in the order. The people were quite silent because Hezekiah had forbidden them to answer, partly to keep Rabshakeh from saying anything further, and partly so that Sennacherib's ambassadors should be left in complete uncertainty as to what impression their words had made. Clarke gives a different reason, drawn from the character of what had been said: the blasphemy is too barefaced to argue with, and since it is Jehovah who has been insulted and not his hearers, the quarrel may be left to him to avenge.

Henry is careful to say that the silence was not for want of an answer. The commissioners could easily and justly have upbraided the speaker with his master's treachery and breach of faith, and asked what religion encourages a man to hope that such conduct will prosper; at the least they might have given him the hint that Ahab once gave to demands as insolent as these, that a man girding on his harness should not boast as though he had already put it off. But the king had commanded them not to answer, and they kept their instructions. There is a time to keep silence as well as a time to speak, Henry says, and there are men to whom offering anything religious or rational is casting pearls before swine; what, after all, can be said to a madman? He suspects the silence worked on the speaker, making him prouder and more secure, so that his heart was lifted up and hardened to his own destruction, and he draws the practical rule that it is often best to leave such people to rail, a decided expression of abhorrence being the best testimony against them.

The rent clothes are that expression. Clarke explains the custom, that the Hebrews rent their garments on hearing blasphemy because it was the greatest of crimes, immediately affecting the majesty of God, and it was right that a religious people should hold in utmost abhorrence every insult offered to the object of their worship. Keil and Delitzsch read the gesture as grief at words by which not Hezekiah only but still more Jehovah had been blasphemed, and Henry adds the second grief in it, for the despised and afflicted condition of Jerusalem, whose reproach was a burden to the men who carried it. Then they reported faithfully, telling the king the words they had heard so that he might consider what was to be done and what answer should be returned. Clarke traces the chain this sets in motion, since the ambassadors lay the matter before the king as God's representative, the king lays it before the prophet as God's minister, and the prophet lays it before God as the people's mediator; and Henry ends where that leaves them, with the matter left to the Lord, who has all hearts in his hands, and themselves committed to him in humble submission, believing hope and fervent prayer.
